componentIdea.title: Energy in Chemical Processes and Everyday Life

chapterOverview.guidingQuestion: How do food and fuel provide energy? If energy is conserved, why do people say it is produced or used?
chapterOverview.purpose: This component idea helps students make sense of how stored energy which often originates from the Sun, is captured, transformed, and used in everyday life, while recognizing that not all energy remains useful after it is transferred.
chapterOverview.centralIdeas: Energy in the environment exists in forms that are not immediately useful for everyday needs. Producing energy refers to capturing stored energy that often originates from the Sun and converting it to a useful and transportable form (e.g., batteries, food, fuel). Energy is not destroyed as it's used and usually takes less useful forms as it spreads to the environment. Designing a system for efficiency maximizes the useful output of energy conversions and minimizes wastes, costs, and unintended impacts.

K-2.nrcQuote: By the end of grade 2. When two objects rub against each other, this interaction is called friction. Friction between two surfaces can warm both of them (e.g., rubbing hands together). There are ways to reduce the friction between two objects. -- NRC, 2012
K-2.progression:
Young children enter school with a strong awareness that the Sun can make them feel warm and that warmth is often connected to comfort or activity. They may also notice that their bodies feel warmer after they run or that objects get warm when they are rubbed. These everyday observations provide the foundation for introducing energy ideas through the concept of warmth.

In grades K--2, the primary advance is recognizing that objects can be made warm through actions such as rubbing---an observable effect of friction. This connects to students' growing understanding of energy in the context of everyday contexts. While students do not yet formally study energy, the idea that warmth results from physical interaction introduces them to the notion of energy transfer in a concrete, sensory-rich way.

This learning is appropriate at this stage because other component ideas (PS3.B) also focus on warmth as a sign of energy movement. Students explore how the Sun warms objects and now see how objects can be warmed by interaction with each other (PS3.D), helping them unify experiences of natural and human-caused warming.

Instruction should prioritize hands-on opportunities where students feel or observe warming through friction such as rubbing hands, dragging blocks while engaging in rich conversation about what they notice. Adding soap makes students\' hands feel \"slippery,\" and eliminates the warming effect. Describing the change in temperature and predicting when warming will or won't happen supports early use of science and engineering practices.

Students may believe that by rubbing things together they are "producing warmth." This thinking sounds like everyday language which describes that windmills or solar panels make energy. Over time the goal of this component idea is to help students understand that these are all examples of capturing and transforming energy that is already present somewhere. For example, the warmth created when rubbing their hands together comes from the energy they received from the food they ate.

3-5.nrcQuote:
By the end of grade 5. The expression "produce energy" typically refers to the conversion of stored energy into a desired form for practical use---for example, the stored energy of water behind a dam is released so that it flows downhill and drives a turbine generator to produce electricity. Food and fuel also release energy when they are digested or burned. When machines or animals "use" energy (e.g., to move around), most often the energy is transferred to heat the surrounding environment.

The energy released by burning fuel or digesting food was once energy from the sun that was captured by plants in the chemical process that forms plant matter (from air and water). (Boundary: The fact that plants capture energy from sunlight is introduced at this grade level, but details of photosynthesis are not.)

It is important to be able to concentrate energy so that it is available for use where and when it is needed. For example, batteries are physically transportable energy storage devices, whereas electricity generated by power plants is transferred from place to place through distribution systems. -- NRC, 2012
3-5.progression:
By grades 3--5, students have had many everyday experiences with devices that run out of power, like flashlights with dead batteries or devices that need to be charged. These experiences reinforce the inaccurate idea that energy can be used up or disappear. At the same time, they begin learning from other component ideas that energy flows through systems and is conserved. This creates an important opportunity to connect everyday language, like \"using energy,\" to the scientific understanding that energy is converted from one form to another.

The key advance in this grade band is the idea that energy can be stored and then released to do something useful. Students explore familiar sources like batteries, food, and fuel and learn that these store energy that can be converted into motion, light, sound, or heat. Some of these energy uses are intended, but unintended flows of energy are unavoidable. They also begin to trace energy back to its original source, usually the Sun. This could include the energy plants capture to put into the food we eat or even the accumulation of water above a dam that is driven by rain tracing back to evaporation caused by the Sun. 

Teachers should directly address common expressions like \"the battery died\" or \"we ran out of energy\" to guide students toward more precise thinking. A more accurate idea is that the battery no longer has stored energy that can be converted. Hands-on activities should allow students to store energy (e.g., winding a toy or charging a device) and observe its release through change or motion.

These early understandings of stored and released energy become critical when students later explore energy storage and release through chemical reactions. In middle school, they will build on these ideas to understand that the rearrangement of atoms in fuels and food is what releases the energy we observe in combustion and digestion.

6-8.nrcQuote:
By the end of grade 8. The chemical reaction by which plants produce complex food molecules (sugars) requires an energy input (i.e., from sunlight) to occur. In this reaction, carbon dioxide and water combine to form carbon-based organic molecules and release oxygen. (Boundary: Further details of the photosynthesis process are not taught at this grade level.)

Both the burning of fuel and cellular digestion in plants and animals involve chemical reactions with oxygen that release stored energy. In these processes, complex molecules containing carbon react with oxygen to produce carbon dioxide and other materials.

Machines can be made more efficient, that is, require less fuel input to perform a given task, by reducing friction between their moving parts and through aerodynamic design. Friction increases energy transfer to the surrounding environment by heating the affected materials. -- NRC, 2012
6-8.progression:
Before middle school, students encounter many everyday examples of energy being stored and released, beginning that happens warming when surfaces rub and advancing to batteries powering devices or food fueling their bodies. Instruction in grades 3-5 should have reduced the number of students who hold the inaccurate idea that energy gets \"used up\" or disappears. They have observed everyday situations where energy appears to run out, like a phone battery dying or a toy slowing down and have created stories of to explain energy flows during the use of these devices. Students have discussed the way that friction causes devices to warm a less useful form of energy.

In grades 6--8, students apply their new knowledge that matter is made of elements and that the rearrangement of atoms in chemical reactions is what causes energy to be released or absorbed. This helps explain that food and fuel provide energy because they contain groupings of atoms that can be released when the atoms are rearranged. Students also learn why other substances, like water or carbon dioxide, do not provide energy when consumed: their atoms are already in low-energy arrangements.

This helps explain why food and fuel provide energy---because they contain molecules that store energy that can be released when the atoms are rearranged. Students also learn why other substances, like water or carbon dioxide, do not provide energy when consumed: their atoms are already in low-energy arrangements.

This deepens students' understanding of what it means to \"release energy\" in everyday life, such as burning wood, digesting food, or powering machines. It also helps expand their view of energy flow---not just from the Sun to food, but from the Sun to nearly all sources of usable energy. Students begin to see that fossil fuels, like food, store energy that originally came from the Sun. Ancient plants captured sunlight through photosynthesis, and over millions of years, their stored energy became concentrated in coal, oil, and natural gas. This perspective helps unify their understanding of energy across both living systems and human technologies, showing that the Sun is the original source of most usable energy on Earth.

During instruction, students can explore and use real-world examples---such as food labels, fuels, or common chemical changes---to highlight the types of reactions used in living and physical systems. Discussions should also include why not all substances release energy, even if they are important to health or function.

These understandings set the stage for high school learning, where students will examine multistep energy transformations and evaluate systems in terms of energy efficiency, environmental impact, and sustainability. High school standards introduce

progression.narrative:
In the earliest grades, students experience and discuss energy as warmth. They learn that the Sun can make objects warm and also see that rubbing their hands together creates warmth. This is the first tie between the Sun's energy and energy their own bodies use. This focus on friction provides a concrete, observable starting point for understanding energy transfers in everyday life.

By grades 3--5, instruction begins to explore energy flows. Energy discussions in this grade band focus on energy motion, stored energy, and things like warming, light, and sound as energy losses. They learn food, fuel, batteries, and falling water as common energy sources that are necessary for everyday activities. They also notice that everyday systems experience losses as warmth, light, or sound which are sources that reduce efficiency. The idea that food and fuel are forms of stored energy lays the groundwork for later understanding of chemical reactions.

In middle school, students learn that chemical reactions store energy and release energy. They see how the reactions of photosynthesis capture energy, while the reactions of respiration and combustion release energy. This helps them understand that whether food or fossil fuels, both sets of reactions ultimately got their energy from the Sun. Efficiency conversations begin where students understand that some energy in every transformation becomes less useful as it spreads into the environment, often as heat.

By high school, students are expected to apply conservation of energy principles across complex systems, where a variety of energy transfers are happening among different types of energy. The chemical and physical processes become more complicated and students also consider how the byproducts of energy transfers affect larger systems and real-world decisions.

standards.statement: Make observations and conduct experiments to provide evidence that friction produces heat and reduces or increases the motion of an object.
standards.bigIdea: When surfaces rub they slow down and can create noticeable warmth. (Note: Focus on objects that slide past each other, not rolling objects or wheeled objects.)
scientificIdeas: When two surfaces rub against each other, they can slow down and become warm---this effect is known as friction.
Friction can slow down or stop the motion of objects that are sliding or rolling.
Friction can also warm the surfaces that are rubbing against each other.
Surfaces warm more when friction causes bigger changes in the motion of an object.
Different surfaces create different amounts of friction---rougher surfaces make things slow down more and warm up more.
Friction is greater when surfaces get pressed together harder.
Adding lubricants (like soap or oil) reduces friction and can keep surfaces from warming when they're rubbed together.
Some machines use friction on purpose, like brakes that slow things down. Others should reduce friction, like wheels and axles, so things can keep moving easily.
studentIdeas: Students may think friction only slows things down and not realize it also creates warmth.
They may believe rubbing or moving creates energy from nothing, rather than changing motion into heat.
Some students assume all friction is bad or should be avoided, not recognizing that some machines rely on friction to work.
Students may think that all surfaces create the same amount of friction or that friction is always the same, regardless of surface texture or pressure.

standards.statement: Describe how energy can be converted into another form for practical use in a system.
standards.bigIdea: In living and mechanical systems, stored energy can be released as heat or converted into motion to accomplish useful tasks. Energy does not disappear, it changes forms within a system and often spreads to the surroundings as heat.
scientificIdeas: Energy can be stored in materials (e.g., batteries, fuels, stretched rubber bands, water behind a dam).
Stored energy can be released and converted into motion (e.g., e-bikes, a person running).
Stored energy can be released and converted for heating (e.g., burning wood, rubbing hands together).
When something changes motion or warms up, energy has been transferred to it.
In most systems, some of the energy involved in motion eventually spreads out as heat to the surroundings.
Living things convert stored energy to motion and heat.
Mechanical devices convert stored energy into motion, often involving electricity (e.g., batteries, generators).
Electricity transfers energy from one place to another so that it can be converted into motion, light, sound, or heat.
The energy in food originally came from the Sun and was captured by plants from sunlight.
studentIdeas: A battery contains electricity (vs stored energy).
Energy gets "used up" (rather than converted to another form).
Energy comes from fuels like gasoline, or from electricity, but not from food.
When something stops moving, it no longer has energy.

standards.statement: Develop a model to explain how food is utilized through chemical reactions to form new molecules that support growth, resulting in the release of energy as matter moves through an organism.
standards.bigIdea: Food is made of groups of atoms that store energy from the Sun. That energy can be released to support movement, growth, and life functions.
scientificIdeas: "Food" is either plant matter or the tissues of organisms that consume plants.
Food is made of carbon-based molecules (primarily carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen) atoms originally assembled by plants using energy from the Sun.
Since different groups of atoms store different amounts of energy, rearrangements of atoms will either capture or release energy.
When food molecules are broken down and rearranged, energy is released and used by the organism.
All compounds contain stored energy, but living systems are only able to perform reactions to release energy from a small set of carbon-based molecules.
The energy in food ultimately came from sunlight, captured by plants through photosynthesis.

Some plant and animal tissues are not eaten by consumers or broken down by decomposers. The energy stored in these tissues has the potential to undergo transformations over immense spans of time and become fossil fuels.
studentIdeas: Food is only used for growth.
All chemicals are useful sources for energy. We choose not to eat some of them because they're poisonous.
Some students believe energy is added to the body by food without recognizing that a chemical process is required to release it.
All substances we consume (e.g., water, vitamins) provide energy.
